title: Fitting PVC fascia board over a rotted timber fascia
subtitle: Cap a weathered or rotted timber fascia board with a uPVC over-fascia to restore the roofline appearance
excerpt: How to cap a rotted or weathered timber fascia board with a uPVC over-fascia capping. Covers inspecting and treating the old fascia, trimming the tile or felt overhang, cutting and fixing the PVC capping, and joining lengths.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK roofline trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A uPVC profile designed to clip or nail over an existing timber fascia board without removing it. The capping is sized to be slightly wider and deeper than standard fascia board dimensions (typically 150 x 10 mm or 175 x 10 mm) and covers the old timber completely, giving a clean white finish and preventing further weathering of the timber beneath.

The horizontal board fixed to the ends of the roof rafters below the roof tiles or slates. The fascia carries the guttering brackets and encloses the eaves. Fascia boards are exposed to weather and rot most quickly at the joints and at the bottom edge where water pools.

content.text: without removing it. It restores the roofline appearance without scaffolding-intensive full replacement. Work from a roof ladder or scaffold tower; do not lean a ladder directly against the guttering.
Inspect and treat the old fascia

Before fitting the capping, remove the guttering and bracket from the front face of the fascia. Check the old timber for rot by prodding with a screwdriver. Surface rot and weathering do not prevent capping, but active wet rot with soft, spongy timber should be cut back and filled with exterior wood filler or the affected section replaced with new timber before capping. Apply a timber preservative to any bare wood or cut ends.
Trim the tile or felt overhang

The top edge of the over-fascia must slide up behind the roof tiles or felt. On some roofs the tiles or felt drape down over the fascia top edge. Lift the bottom course of tiles carefully and trim back any felt overhang with a utility knife to allow the top lip of the capping to insert 10 to 15 mm behind the tiles. Replace the tiles before fixing the capping.
Cut and fix the capping lengths

Cut the uPVC capping to length with a fine-toothed crosscut saw or a mitre saw. For external corners, mitre-cut both pieces at 45 degrees. Start at one gable end and work along the run, sliding the top lip behind the tile drip edge and pressing the face of the capping flat against the old fascia. Fix with 25 mm stainless lost-head nails at 600 mm centres, nailing through the face into the old timber fascia. Use a nail punch to set the nail heads just below the surface.
Join lengths and refit the guttering

Join adjacent lengths with a uPVC fascia joining strip, which clips over the butted join. Allow a 3 mm expansion gap at each join to allow for thermal movement. Refit guttering brackets, screwing through the uPVC capping and into the old fascia timber behind.

attrs.symptom: Capping bows away from the fascia between fixings
attrs.cause: Fixing centres too wide, or capping fitted in cold weather and expanded once warm.
attrs.fix: Reduce nail spacing to 300 mm. In warm weather the capping will tighten against the fascia; in cold weather ensure the expansion gap is maintained.

attrs.symptom: Guttering bracket screws will not grip after refitting
attrs.cause: Screws too short to reach through the capping and into the old fascia.
attrs.fix: Use screws at least 60 mm long for guttering brackets to penetrate through the capping and into the rafter behind the fascia.
